body: With the idea of Joe Looney from Rare Pepe Wallet and organized by R.A.R.E, this milestone event in NFT history kicked off in January 2018 with a huge event in this story: RARE AF #1 NYC, the first Rare Art Festival.

While total attendance was low, some of the most prominent people in the burgeoning Crypto Art space appeared, including Matt Hall and John Watkinson from Cryptopunks and Beatriz Ramos from DADA NYC, in addition to Looney. According to Jason Bailey, it was a challenge getting enough artists to participate. Ramos spoke about the event on Right Click Save saying:

“I remember the feeling of effervescence, of excitement — a vital energy that day that felt like the festival was a catalyst for something big. It felt like we all knew that we were on the verge of something huge that no one else was aware of, in a room with other people who share this feeling.”
She continued, reflecting on the legacy of the event after four years:

“I think it catalyzed the NFT movement — the creative ferment, innovation, experimentation, and community but at the same time it buried it, becoming a movement that was purely market driven. The movement in itself (which is not ideological or aesthetic) ended up transforming into the beginnings of a market. And what is left to the community is a shared sense of nostalgia for those of us who lived that moment.”

body: In 2017 Robbie Barrat began using Generative Adversarial Networks to make art, producing his first two significant bodies of work, Landscapes and Nude Portraits, which reached collectors in 2018. He had begun his explorations of AI in 2016, with a Bach-imitating LSTM in July and a rapping neural network in November. His initial attempt with landscapes yielded realistic but ultimately unremarkable results, highlighting the limitations of merely replicating traditional art forms with new technology. Seeking deeper engagement with the medium, Barrat then focused on nude portraits, intentionally guiding the GAN to misinterpret the overall structure while correctly learning local features. This approach underscored his interest in the creative potential of GANs, allowing the machine to produce unexpected and intriguing generative outcomes beyond pre-programmed rules. While these works remain central to his artistic exploration and explanations, they—in particular Nude Portraits—have played a remarkable role in the history of the birth of NFTs, as we will see later this year, but also its uglier speculation and mania, which ultimately drove Barrat to disavow them.

img.credit: Robbie Barrat, sample output from nude-portrait GAN, art-DCGAN, 2018. Courtesy of the artist, via the artist's GitHub repository.

body: Christie’s inaugurated its Art+Tech Summit at its London headquarters on July 18. The now-annual initiative, hosted in collaboration with Christie’s Education, aimed to explore the intersection of technology and the art world, specifically blockchain technology, following the cryptocurrency spike in price in 2018. The inaugural conference’s topic was “Exploring Blockchain – Is the Art World Ready for Consensus?” and featured thought leaders like Hans Ulrich Obrist and Jason Bailey. Infamously, Christie’s gave away 300 Robbie Barrat NFTs of “generated nude #7” on physical cards in a gift bag to attendees, placed in the bags by SuperRare in collaboration with Bailey and Barrat. Perhaps expecting greater blockchain literacy, the reception of the tokens was disappointing, as according to SuperRare’s John Crain, “We were genuinely excited about the idea, only to find out the next day that literally no one understood what the tokenized card was for.” With SuperRare reporting only 12 of the 300 ever claimed, the remaining pieces today are known as the “Lost Robbies” and—against the initial desires or interest of the artist—sell for hundreds of thousands of dollars. One is featured in the Le Random collection.

img.cap: A panel photograph from the inaugural Christie's Art+Tech Summit in London, with Hans Ulrich Obrist among the speakers.
img.credit: Georgina Adam, Hans Ulrich Obrist, Sylvie Gleises, Kati Price and Richard Entrup on stage at Christie's Art+Tech Summit, London, 18 July 2018. Whitewall.

body: In April, SuperRare, one of the oldest surviving crypto art marketplaces, launched its beta smart contract on the Ethereum blockchain. Founded by a small team in Brooklyn, SuperRare aimed to make art collecting as accessible as buying stocks or posting photos online. Inspired by projects previously covered on this Timeline like CryptoPunks and Rare Pepe Wallet, SuperRare enabled select artists to issue art work on their platform. The platform quickly garnered interest, with Jason Bailey making the first purchases from Robbie Barrat’s AI Generated Nude Portrait series. Later in the year—and this Timeline—Bailey, Barrat and SuperRare would give away 300 of these pieces in person at Christie’s First Art + Tech Summit, the infamous Lost Robbies. SuperRare was only modestly successful in its first year, facilitating over 1,124 primary sales yet only $91,000 in first-year sales volume and around 550 ETH in total volume. These muted figures demonstrate—even in the ninth chapter—how early we still are in this story. The platform’s release, however, marks a significant milestone in the story of generative art in this decade.

The project was watched closely, as it had been one of the largest ICOs at the time. Tezos—now in the hands of its decentralized community—would spend the next 18 months steadily releasing updates and proving the viability of its consensus mechanism. It will reappear in the next decade—and chapter—in March 2020 when the first signs of creative life appear on the chain and, of course, one year later in March 2021 with the launch of Hic et Nunc.

body: An indication, like in 2001, that institutions—forced apparently largely to be reactionary—are willing to show interest in digital art following a catalyst that sparks renewed public interest. This time period provided just that, as following a steep rise in cryptocurrency prices at the end of 2017 and into 2018, it is perhaps not a coincidence that the remainder of 2018 saw renewed institutional interest from entrants like The Whitney, The V&A and Christie’s. body: William Entriken, Dieter Shirley, Jacob Evans and Nastassia Sachs authored the ERC-721 protocol, proposed in January 2018 as Ethereum’s first NFT token standard, laying the foundation for the variety of ways NFTs remain used to this day. ERC-721 defines a set of guidelines for creating NFTs to represent unique digital assets. The protocol stipulates that, unlike fungible tokens, NFTs cannot be exchanged on a one-to-one basis due to their distinct properties. The standard facilitated the creation, transfer and management of unique digital items, enabling their increased use in creative fields such as fine art and gaming.

body: While first exhibited in January 2019 at Madrid’s Colección SOLO, Memories of Passersby I is an AI artwork generating an endless stream of unique, real-time portraits. A fully autonomous physical installation, the work features a neural network of multiple GANs housed in a chestnut wood cabinet, linked to two framed screens. Unlike traditional generative art, it does not rely on a database but continuously creates new images pixel by pixel, ensuring no repetition. Klingemann trained the AI using 17th- to 19th-century portraits and his surrealist aesthetic preferences. The work would go on to be sold by Sotheby’s in March 2019, a continued indication of institutional interest in AI art.

img.cap: Sotheby's catalogue image of Memories of Passersby I: the chestnut wood console with its two framed screens showing the continuously generated portraits.
img.credit: Mario Klingemann, Memories of Passersby I, 2018. Sotheby's, Contemporary Art Day Auction, London, 6 March 2019, lot 109.

body: In Tyler Hobbs’s first exhibition, Progress, the artist examines the profound impact of computers and technology on contemporary life, emphasizing the necessity for artists to directly engage with these tools. These programmatic works further demonstrate what this Timeline has shown for decades: interacting with computers in their native form can produce uniquely crafted artwork that is inherently infused with the essence of the latest technology. Hobbs had been creating and sharing his practice online since 2014. Progress can thus be seen as a literal marker for Hobbs’s artistic development over the previous 4-5 years. The work showcases the culmination of Hobbs’s thought and development up to this point, a key moment in generative art in the 2010s.

img.cap: Installation view of Tyler Hobbs's first exhibition, Progress: four framed generative prints hung on a concrete wall beside the gallery's window.
img.credit: Tyler Hobbs, Progress, Galeria dos Topos, Leon, Mexico, 2018. Courtesy of the artist.

body: Ian Cheng introduced BOB (Bag of Beliefs), a pioneering artificial life form depicted as a chimeric branching serpent. BOB represents a significant evolution in Cheng’s exploration of simulation, focusing on an individual agent’s ability to adapt to unexpected situations. Over time, BOB’s body, mind and personality evolve to manage life’s surprises, transforming them into routines. Featuring a composite AI architecture with various “demons” that drive its behavior, BOB learns rule-based beliefs from sensory experiences. This dynamic interaction between sub-personalities and external stimuli highlights the intricate relationship between technology, autonomy and human-like adaptability in generative art.

img.cap: Installation view of BOB at the Serpentine Galleries: the projected creature on the gallery wall with a visitor viewing it through the accompanying phone app on a handheld mount.
img.credit: Ian Cheng, BOB (Bag of Beliefs), 2018. Installation view, Serpentine Galleries, London. Serpentine Galleries.

body: This AI audiovisual installation explores the transformative forces of nature through real-time algorithmic visuals and AI-composed music. Offering a bird’s-eye view of a dynamic landscape, the project visualizes the shifting behaviors of rivers and their impact on the earth. Utilizing bespoke algorithms and shaders, the installation simulates natural phenomena such as hydraulic erosion and meander scars. The accompanying soundscape, developed with composers kling klang klong using the Google Magenta Performance RNN model, dynamically responds to the river’s simulated movements, creating an immersive experience that underscores the unpredictability and beauty of natural generativity.

img.credit: Courtesy of onformative.

body: Pierre Huyghe’s exploration of early AI technology at the Serpentine Galleries involved a transformative and autonomous art installation based on MRI scans, live animals and intense audience interaction. Huyghe used fMRI technology to capture the brain activity of an individual imagining selected images. This data was processed by a deep neural network attempting to reconstruct the images, resulting in continuously evolving visual representations displayed on large LED screens. The exhibition’s environment was dynamic, influenced by sensors detecting light, temperature, humidity, the presence of insects and even visitors' gazes. Live flies living in the gallery created unique patterns, and the space constantly morphed, embodying an ecosystem where human, animal and technological elements interacted unpredictably, reflecting Huyghe’s vision of art as a self-presenting ritual.

img.cap: Installation view of UUmwelt at the Serpentine: one of the large freestanding LED screens showing a neural-network reconstruction, in a gallery whose walls carry the work's insect-marked surfaces.
img.credit: Pierre Huyghe, UUmwelt, 2018. Installation view, Serpentine Galleries, London. Serpentine Galleries.

body: Chaos Machine demonstrates the breadth and materiality of blockchain-based generative art. Distributed Gallery unveiled the Chaos Machine—a unique crypto-jukebox artwork—during the Proof of Work exhibition at the Schinkel Pavillon in Berlin and curated by Simon Denny in September, 2018. This exhibition featured an eclectic lineup, including CryptoKitties and Harm van den Dorpel. The piece itself was constructed from oak wood, steel, slate, and glass. This 192 cm tall installation burns banknotes to play user-generated music playlists stored on the Ethereum blockchain via IPFS technology. Burning a banknote mints an NFT and prints a QR code, allowing new songs to be added to the playlist. The early material-blockchain generative work has been exhibited in multiple prestigious venues, including the Kate Vass Galerie in Zurich and the FIAC in Paris. These early experiments with NFTs by artists like Simon Denny and Robbie Barrat demonstrate how artist-led the movement was prior to the popularization of NFTs in 2021.

img.cap: The Chaos Machine itself: the oak, steel, slate and glass crypto-jukebox, with its printed receipt roll spooling onto the floor.
img.credit: Distributed Gallery, Chaos Machine, 2018. Courtesy of Distributed Gallery.

body: This mixed-media AI installation autonomously generates images, embodying a self-sustaining “art factory,” an early example of work employing material, coded and AI-generative techniques. Utilizing two flatbed scanners facing each other, the installation employs a computer script to create random settings and initiate scanning.

Deep-learning algorithms then analyze the images and are “validated as art” if they match existing works by over 83%. These images were shared on social platforms and were occasionally printed live in the gallery. This work explores technological automation, object agency and the economics of art production, reflecting on the continuous, independent creation of cultural artifacts.

img.cap: Installation view of the work: machine-generated images hung as prints on the gallery wall behind the desktop computer that runs the scanning system.
img.credit: Adam Basanta, All We'd Ever Need Is One Another, 2018. Courtesy of the artist.

body: This autonomous kinetic installation explores self-organization and emergent complex behavior based on a reimagination of cybernetic art in the twenty-first century. Comprising 1250 stepper motors arranged in a two-by-two-meter grid, each motor is equipped with a white acrylic pointer. These pointers move in response to alternating current, initially in random directions, reversing upon collision. This interaction creates complex, evolving patterns on the installation’s surface, reflecting non-hierarchical communication and collective behavior. Inspired by Alvin Toffler’s notion of reassembling fragmented problems, Baecker’s work serves as a contemporary synthesis of cybernetic, kinetic and generative art, thus paying homage to three critical roots of all digital art, all mentioned many times in this Timeline.

img.cap: Installation view of the two-by-two-metre grid of 1,250 stepper motors, each carrying a white acrylic pointer.

body: One of the first works by artist duo Operator, On View captures the spirit of their practice, which uses digital tools to question—along with Lauren Lee McCarthy and Sougwen Chung—the most pressing issues facing humans and technology. Created by Operator’s Ania Catherine and Dejha Ti and commissioned by the SCAD Museum of Art, On View is an immersive experiential artwork that critiques modern society’s obsession with becoming the subject of art. The piece questions the implications of addictive interfaces, surveillance capitalism and data privacy. Utilizing TouchDesigner, real-time facial recognition, voice commands and environmental sensors, On View integrates advanced technology seamlessly into its physical spaces. This installation invites participants to critically engage with the digital architectures shaping our realities, emphasizing the need for tech literacy as technology becomes increasingly invisible.

img.cap: Installation view of Operator's On View at the SCAD Museum of Art: a darkened gallery with a lit circular plinth and a figure reflected in a curved mirrored wall.
img.credit: Operator (Ania Catherine and Dejha Ti), On View, 2019. Installation view, SCAD Museum of Art. Courtesy of the artists, operator.la.

body: A seminal event in generative art history stands as April’s release of Autoglyphs by Larva Labs. Considered the first on-chain generative art on the Ethereum blockchain, each unique glyph was created by code running directly on the blockchain, making them self-contained and independent of any central authority.

Matt Hall and John Watkinson’s Autoglyphs were inspired by the pair’s admiration for Sol LeWitt’s Wall Drawings. The famed series would go on to inspire Erick Calderon to launch Art Blocks in November 2020, roughly 18 months after the release of Autoglyphs.

Anyone could generate an Autoglyph by donating 0.2Ξ to the charity 350.org, with a total of 512 glyphs produced before the generator ceased operation. The first long-form generative series on Ethereum was thus directly inspired by the art historical legacy of rules-based systems thinking in Sol LeWitt. Its primary sales went to charity. Thus, as with the invention of NFTs themselves, the roots of long-form generative remain distant from the speculative mania and unsavory associations that would later plague NFTs broadly.

Critically, Autoglyphs helped establish the concept that artwork and ownership details could be embedded on blockchains, ensuring long-term and public provenance. This project forever stands as a unique, critical link between the legacy of Conceptualism and systems-based thinking and where we stand today with on-chain art.

Commissioned by the Whitney for its artport site, this work is one of the first to engage with blockchain technology to make its way to a museum’s permanent collection. The work in this way is an entire reimagination of the relationship between artwork, museum and audience. Acquired by the Whitney Museum’s Christiane Paul, this piece’s incorporation of blockchain technology allow the market life of the work to continue beyond its acquisition. Fifty NFTs, dubbed digital certificates by the museum, linked to the artwork, were given to donors who could freely transfer or sell them. As these certificates change hands, the evolving list of donors is tracked on the museum’s website. Additionally, the artwork itself contains a blockchain key, making the first audience member to discover it the fifty-first donor.

body: Casey Reas’s precursor to Feral File was inspired by Harm van den Dorpel’s Left Gallery from 2015. Named a2p (artist-to-peer) and built on Bitmark with Sean Moss-Pultz, it was Reas’s early exploration of blockchain, promoting peer-to-peer art trading. In each iteration, three to four curators invited 25 artists, who minted one original artwork as an edition of 10 plus one artist proof. Over a week, artists curated their collections by swapping artworks, all recorded on the blockchain, with lively discussion reminiscent of IRC chats. A2p stands as a critical moment in this history because, in many ways, it helped legitimize the blockchain for pre-blockchain generative artists. For many, a2p marked their initial foray into NFTs, inextricably linking generative art and blockchains. The platform did more than introduce; it ignited a curiosity that set the stage for the increase in interest that was to come while laying the groundwork for Reas’s Feral File.

img.credit: Courtesy of Casey Reas.

body: The exhibition Automat und Mensch: A History of AI and Generative Art in May 2019 anticipated the arrival of AI and generative art. The audacious show at Kate Vass Galerie was organized by Kate Vass and curated by Jason Bailey (Artnome) and Georg Bak. Vass told this author about the show: “The whole show was actually an attempt to highlight the historical perspective of generative art and the predecessors of AI.” Going back several decades, the show spotlighted the historical roots of AI and generative art: cybernetics and early robotics, as well as the computer art of pioneers like Frieder Nake and Herbert W. Franke. The show also includes contemporary artists. Bak told me:

“As Kate said, our aim was to reflect on the history of AI—from early generative art to the most recent developments in AI with DeepDream and GANs. We actually had Larva Labs in the show with physical Autoglyphs. John [Watkinson] told me last time I saw him that we actually pushed him to finish Autoglyphs to get it ready for the show. It was also interesting that we actually had the first on-chain NFT in this exhibition. There were some very recent developments as well as the historical context.”
Bailey spoke to this author (Peter Bauman) about the relevance of the exhibition five years later, saying:
“I was trying to get my heroes to agree to do this.

I don’t think that’s an exaggeration. I had spent twenty years looking up to people like Casey Reas, Jared Tarbell and John Maeda. I was lucky enough that I had been several years into writing the Artnome blog, where people were at least somewhat aware that I had been passionately—for no real profit or commercial purpose—writing about art and technology out of something that I love. That opened the door to at least getting responses to some emails. There was some strategy to trying to get the folks that I had been in more recent contact with who were maybe slightly better known names. Then, when you went further along, you could say, “Well, so and so has signed up.” Everyone wants to know who’s already agreed but you have to get the first few people to agree to be able to get the additional people to agree.

It’s not an accident that we’re talking about it five years later. I think it’s a reflection of the attention to detail and the effort. I wouldn’t have anticipated—as someone who’d just started to curate—the effort that it took.”

body: This large-scale immersive audiovisual installation marked Anadol’s first major installation in New York City, and extended the machine learning practice he had begun with Archive Dreaming in 2017. Using machine learning algorithms on a vast dataset of over 100 million architectural images of New York City, Anadol created a cinematic data universe. The experience revealed the city’s collective memories and AI’s ability to re-imagine, blending architecture with perceptions of time and space. The installation offered a glimpse into the future of AI-enhanced immersive installations for which Anadol is now known after 2022’s Unsupervised at MoMA.

body: The software engineer Sarin, formerly of Bell Labs, began her experiments with GANs in early 2018. This Twitter post from March 2018 shows an example of possibly her earliest public work. Just a year later, Sarin had already began standing out with work suggesting the surreal. By the end of 2018, Sarin spoke to Jason Bailey about her practice on his Artnome blog.

2019 saw Sarin’s first exhibition, which included this work, part of her #latentDoodles series. It was showcased at the Computer Vision Art Gallery during ICCV 2019 in Seoul, Korea. The work explores the human-like quality of hand-drawn marks with the distinct patterns of computational creation. Using SNGAN trained on her sketches and doodles, Sarin upscaled and colorized the image with cycleGAN for added texture. Sarin enhances the abstract images with carefully crafted captions, adding a verbal layer that deepens the folk-like yet computationally intricate nature of her work. The work exemplifies Sarin’s master from an early of coaxing the traditional and human out of modern AI techniques.

img.cap: Helena Sarin's GAN work Inferno as published on its exhibition page in the 2019 Computer Vision Art Gallery, the show in which it was exhibited.
img.credit: Helena Sarin, Inferno, 2019. Computer Vision Art Gallery, CVPR 2019.

body: This large-scale Rhizomatiks installation and dance performance, with technical and creative direction by Daito Manabe and choreography by MIKIKO, was held at the Tokyo FESTIVAL. Situated in Tokyo’s Shiba district, the project interweaves light and sound at the Daihonzan Zojoji Temple. There, architectural and topographical data were coded into a virtual space, which was then translated into dynamic light and sound emitted by balloon-shaped devices. Audience movements influenced these devices, creating an interactive experience. The work—like much in this decade—showcases many of the forebearers of digital art, including lumino-kinetic sculpture, participation and gernativity.

body: This data art project that visualizes cybersecurity threat data as a series of algorithmically generated images and a 4K animation. The work features three main components: black obelisks representing threats, an organic mesh symbolizing the detection system and flowing strands illustrating the creativity enabled by neutralized threats. Each mesh shape, generated by a unique algorithm, corresponds to five different industries: media, banking, government, technology and retail. Debuted at the RSA Conference in San Francisco, the project is a key example of the renewed interest in data visualization art that was propelled—in part—in the previous decade by Ben Fry’s work and his cocreation of Processing.

img.credit: Courtesy of Brendan Dawes.

body: Running until the summer of 2022, Rare AF was the original on-chain art event that paved the way for Bright Moments, Proof of People and the variety of other Web3 native art events that now dot the yearly social calendar. In May 2019, finding enough collectors was the real challenge, echoing similar sentiment for 2024, despite a rapid jump in interest in the intervening 5 years. This 2019 iteration was the second and continued the momentum from year, featuring the space’s significant builders; however, the event would prove small until NFTs took off the following years.

img.cap: Rhea Myers's Tokens Equal Text, one of the works shown and sold at the second Rare Digital Art Festival in Bushwick, Brooklyn, on 18 May 2019; this is the artwork, not a photograph of the festival.
img.credit: Rhea Myers, Tokens Equal Text, 2019. Licensed CC BY-SA 4.0, rhea.art.

body: May saw another legendary blockchain art event with the first annual Contemporary and Digital Art Fair (CADAF) in New York City. The show itself featured Artxcode’s show of algorithmic work by then-essentially unknown artists Dmitri Cherniak and Tyler Hobbs. The pair would make names for themselves the following decade and chapter with their releases on Art Blocks. Other artists whose work has been exhibited include Kevin Abosch. Panelists at the event were impressive, including Ania Catherine and Dejha Ti from Operator, Jason Bailey (Artnome), John Watkinson and Le Random advisor Georg Bak.

img.cap: A photograph from the inaugural CADAF in New York: a five-person CADAF Talks panel on stage beneath the fair's illuminated CADAF.ART sign.
img.credit: CADAF Talks panel at the first Contemporary and Digital Art Fair (CADAF), Lightbox NYC, New York, May 2019. CADAF, via the Internet Archive.

body: This early example of a neural net animated narrative by Tyka blends the aesthetics of a moving painting with the structure of a music video. Created entirely using artificial neural networks, the visuals were generated with BigGAN. The animation explores the narrative potential of GANs, offering a contemplative reflection on humanity’s brief existence and our relationship with nature on geological timescales. EONS emphasizes the emotional incomprehensibility of our scientific knowledge, inviting viewers to ponder our place within the vast expanse of time.

img.cap: A still frame from Mike Tyka's BigGAN-generated animation EONS, taken from the artist's own Vimeo upload of the work.
img.credit: Mike Tyka, EONS, 2019 (video still). Courtesy of the artist.

body: As we close the decade, the proliferation of AI art combined with NFTs means that tracking every significant piece by every relevant artist is extremely challenging. Here are relevant works and artists deserving of recognition from the decade: Lulu xXX & Noj Barke’s photogrammetry Erik Swahn’s StyleGAN experiments Tom White’s work with Convolutional Neural Network classifiers Anna Ridler’s early training sets (e.g. Myriad) David Young’s work with flowers and GANs Runway Palette by Cyril Diagne

body: “OpenAI releases a paper on GPT-2 (Generative Pre-trained Transformer), an AI-powered text generation model trained on vast amounts of written text sourced via the internet; users are able to download and even fine-tune a smaller version of the model. Soon after, Gwern Branwen publishes seminal poetry experiments using GPT-2, Parrish’s Gutenberg Poetry Corpus, and Adam Daniel King releases Talk to Transformer, a no-code text generation interface.”
-Sasha Stiles
